description: Layer 2: bulk copy as tar over exec (FILES-OVER-EXEC.md 5.8): trees up and down, hostile archives, and the environments that refuse. Generated by tools/gen_bulk.py.

scenarios.description: Names with spaces, newlines, quotes, shell syntax, a leading dash, unicode and lengths beyond 100 and 255 bytes survive upload and download, and no name is interpreted by a shell.

Empty directories, permission bits (including a read-only directory that still holds files), mtimes, and symbolic links of every shape (relative, to a directory, dangling, absolute, upward, very long) come back exactly; links are stored by their target text and never followed.
A 50 MiB file (and a small one) goes up in several chunks and comes back byte for byte: the digest is the file's, and no stage file is left beside the destination.
With a small chunk size the upload goes through the stage (several appends, then one extraction) and ends the same as a one-request upload; the stage is gone.
An archive that is exactly one chunk long is sent staged with an empty tail that is not sent, and extracts.
A list of sources uploads each by its base name (a file, a directory with its tree) and only those.
Uploading into a directory that exists keeps what is there, replaces files of the same name, and does not change the directory's own mode.
The destination may be several levels below an existing directory.
An empty directory uploads as an empty destination.
A trailing slash on the destination names the same directory.
A destination that is a file is not_a_directory, and the file is not touched.
A destination below a file is not_a_directory and creates nothing.
A relative destination, the root, and a source that cannot be archived are invalid_request before anything is sent.
Downloading a path that does not exist is not_found and writes nothing.
Downloading one file puts it in the local directory under its base name; a file whose name starts with a dash works.
An empty directory downloads as nothing.
Symbolic links in the sandbox come down as links (to a file, to a directory, dangling, absolute, pointing out), never as the content they point at, and hard links come down as files.

args: cd "$1" && ln a hard && ln -s /etc/passwd abs && ln -s .. up && ln -s nowhere dangling && ln -s dir dirlink

scenarios.description: A file the sandbox user may not read fails the download with permission_denied; the error is reported, not a partial success.
Extraction merges into a local directory that exists: other files stay, same-named files are replaced.
A local symbolic link in the way of a downloaded file is replaced by the file; what it pointed at is not written (the driver fails the op if it was).
A member named with `..` is refused (protocol, `unsafe archive member`) and nothing is written outside the target, whatever its position in the name.
An absolute member name is refused.
Nothing is written through a symbolic link: not one the archive made earlier, not one that was already in the target; a link in the way of a directory member is replaced by the directory.
A symlink member is created as it says, whatever it points at, because it is never followed; a hard link is made only to a regular file the archive wrote, and never to anything else.
A device or FIFO member is io (unsupported member type); a header with a bad checksum, and an archive cut off before its end, are protocol errors.
Empty and `.` components are dropped, the root member sets nothing, set-id bits are not carried, a directory's mode is applied after its content, and a file is created owner-writable first.
A file member over a local directory is is_directory and the directory stays.
Archives written as GNU tar (long names with `L`/`K`), as pax (`path`, `linkpath`), and as ustar with a `prefix` field extract the same.
Uploading to a read-only filesystem is an error that names it, creates nothing, and leaves what was there.
Uploading to a directory the sandbox user may not write is permission_denied, and the old file is intact.
A destination filesystem that fills up fails the upload with io (No space left on device); a destination this call created is removed, a stage is removed, and the filesystem works again.
A tree one client uploads is the tree another client downloads: each client reads the tar the other one wrote, and the sandbox's `tar` accepts it.
